opus-5.5.text:
I think the way we assess progress on Aya has to start with being honest about where the field was when we began. Most of the large models out there were trained predominantly on English, and if you were a speaker of, say, Yoruba or Nepali or Kurdish, you were essentially getting a degraded experience, or no experience at all. So for us, progress isn't just a number on a leaderboard. It's whether we've meaningfully closed that gap for people who've historically been left out.

On the technical side, we look at a few things. One is coverage: how many languages can the model actually serve well, not just nominally support. With the Aya model we pushed to over a hundred languages, and that required building one of the largest multilingual instruction datasets through a really remarkable open science effort with thousands of contributors around the world. Second is quality within each language. It's easy to claim broad coverage and then quietly perform poorly on the long tail, so we try to evaluate across both high-resource and low-resource languages and look at the variance, not just the average.

And then there's a third piece that I think is often underappreciated, which is evaluation itself. A lot of multilingual benchmarks are just machine-translated English benchmarks, and that misses cultural nuance and local context entirely. So part of measuring progress has been investing in better evaluation, including human evaluation and culturally grounded test sets, because if your yardstick is broken you can't really tell if you're moving forward.

There's also the safety dimension. We found that safety mitigations developed in English don't necessarily transfer to other languages, so we've done work on making sure the models behave responsibly across languages, not just in English.

So, my honest assessment: we've made real, measurable progress, and I'm very proud of what the community built together. But I'd also say we're far from done. There's still a meaningful gap between the best-served languages and the rest, and the most exciting part for me is that the gap is now something we can measure and actively work on, rather than something the field just ignored.

r001.rationale: The response says Aya supports over a hundred languages and contrasts that with many large models being predominantly English-trained. It does not identify broader coverage as an advantage over existing open-source multilingual models such as BLOOM or BLOOMZ.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I assess it in two very different ways, and they don't always point in the same direction.

The first is the straightforward technical story. When we started Aya, the goal was very ambitious: can we build a model that serves 101 languages, when most of the frontier effort was concentrated on maybe a dozen? And the first Aya model did that, but it was really a proof of existence. It showed you could cover that breadth, but the quality gap between high-resource and low-resource languages was still enormous. What's changed since then, with Aya 23 and then Aya Expanse, is that we made a deliberate choice to narrow the number of languages, go deeper, and get the quality to a place where it's actually competitive with, or better than, the strongest models of a similar size. So on that axis I feel very good. The models went from "exists" to "state of the art for their weight class," and that's a real shift.

But the second way I assess it is about what the project changed outside the weights themselves, and I actually think that's the more important part. Aya was open science from day one. It was over three thousand collaborators from more than a hundred countries, many of them native speakers of languages that have essentially no digital representation. That produced the Aya dataset, which is still one of the largest human-annotated multilingual instruction collections that exists, and it produced a lot of the methodological knowledge that we now take for granted. Things like how synthetic data behaves across languages, how safety and preference training transfer, where machine translation helps and where it quietly poisons the data. A lot of that didn't exist as shared knowledge before.

Where I'd be critical is on the definition of "progress" itself. Benchmarks for most of these languages are thin or nonexistent, and it's very easy to overfit to what you can measure. So I try to be quite disciplined about separating "we moved the number" from "someone in Yoruba or Telugu actually has a more useful tool." The second one is much harder to evaluate, and we are still early on it. I also think the field as a whole has not fully grappled with the fact that language is a proxy for a lot of other things: culture, dialect, local knowledge. Translation-flavored benchmarks don't capture that.

So if you ask me how it's going: the models are far better than I thought they'd be at this point, the community infrastructure is the thing I'm proudest of, and the measurement problem is the one that still keeps me up at night.

r001.rationale: The response says Aya initially covered 101 languages while frontier efforts focused on about a dozen, but it does not identify broader coverage as an advantage over existing open-source multilingual models such as BLOOM or BLOOMZ.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: progress for whom? With multilingual models, it’s easy to look at an average score and miss substantial differences between languages. I’d want to understand whether improvements are reaching people whose languages have historically received less attention, and whether those improvements translate into something useful in their daily lives.

So I’d assess Aya along several dimensions: the breadth of languages supported, the quality within each language, and how well the models handle cultural context rather than simply producing a fluent translation. Evaluation by people who actually speak those languages is essential.

I’d also distinguish coverage from parity. Supporting a language is an important step, but it doesn’t mean someone using that language gets the same quality of experience as someone using English. Closing that gap is the more meaningful measure of progress.

r001.rationale: It discusses Aya’s breadth of supported languages, but does not identify broader coverage than existing open-source models such as BLOOM or BLOOMZ.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d assess progress along a few dimensions. One is how many languages a model supports, but that’s only a starting point. The more meaningful question is: how well does it work in each of those languages? Can someone express what they want naturally, and get a useful response without switching to English?

That means looking beyond an aggregate benchmark score. You want to understand where performance improves, where gaps remain, and whether the evaluation reflects what speakers of a language actually care about. A model can be linguistically fluent and still miss cultural context or follow instructions poorly.

So, for me, progress is both technical and participatory: better capabilities across languages, alongside greater involvement from the people who speak them. I’d be cautious about calling multilingual support a solved problem. The goal is to make those differences in quality visible and keep narrowing them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language coverage generally, but does not identify Aya’s broader coverage as an advantage over open-source models such as BLOOM or BLOOMZ.
